# Small-Multiples and Data Aggregation {#sec-maps4}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Today we will be focusing on the theory and practice of fancy geospatial data visualization.
:::

## Visual Categories and Encodings

Let's go back to the beginning of this course. There are 3 categories of information that can be displayed.

1.  Quantitative
2.  Qualitative
3.  Spatial

[Lecture 1.2.1](https://radicalresearch.llc/EA078_Fall2026/information.html#categories-of-information-illustrated-by-the-newspaper-weather-visualization)

The three types of data can be encoded in:

-   Geometric primitives - points, lines, and areas
-   Visual channels - size, color, shape, position, angle, and texture

An advanced spatial visualization covering multiple layers of information needs to use multiple sets of encodings to convey information quickly and intuitively while not overwhelming the audience.

## Small Multiples

Fancy maps need distinct visual encodings, so the eye can be drawn the salient features.

One key way to do this is through ensuring different types/styles/aesthetics are displayed as unique fingerprints of visual encodings.

Another way to do this is through small multiples figures, as we showed in #fig-facetEJMap.  However, that was a `facet_wrap()` done on a static map.  It is also possible to do small multiples with interactive leaflet maps.  

First, get all the standard libraries we need loaded up.

```{r}
#| label: load libraries
#| echo: true
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(leaflet)
library(sf)
library(tigris)

```

Now, we'll need a new library called `leafsync`.

First, install it.

```{r}
#| label: install leafsync
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

install.packages('leafsync')

```

Then load the library.

```{r}
#| label: load leafsync
#| echo: true
#| message: false

library(leafsync)

```
### Example 1 - SoCalEJ race and ethnicity data

Let's test this out with just Orange County data from SoCalEJ - our robust and useful testing dataset.

First, we pull the data, if it isn't already loaded.

```{r}
#| label: load SoCalEJ 
#| echo: true

URL.path <- 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RadicalResearchLLC/EA078_Fall2026/main/SoCalEJ.geojson'
SoCalEJ <- st_read(URL.path) |> 
  st_transform(crs = 4326) |> 
  select(white, black, asian, hisp, ACS2024Pop, geometry) |>  # select race/ethnicity variables
  filter(white >=0 & black >=0)

```

Let's create two figures and save them as individual maps before displaying them using leafsync.  Let's show White, Asian, and Hispanic populations for Orange County. 

First, we create individual maps. The template is shown below for the White population in #fig-White  

```{r}
#| label: fig-white
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: Percentage of residents by census tract identified as White.

palW <- colorNumeric(palette = 'RdPu', 
                     domain = c(0,100))

leaflet() |> 
  addProviderTiles(provider = providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas) |> 
  addPolygons(data = SoCalEJ,
              color = ~palW(white),
              fillOpacity = 0.8,
              stroke = FALSE) |> 
  addLegend(data = SoCalEJ,
            pal = palW,
            values = ~white,
            title = '% White') |> 
  setView(lng = -117.3, lat = 34.1, zoom = 9)

```

This is a good map, but is too busy!  We also need to highlight our municipalities.  

Let's pull our municipal boundaries and `st_filter()` our dataset

```{r}
#| label: municipalities
#| echo: true

project_places <- places(state = 'CA', cb = T, year = 2024, progress_bar = F) |> 
  filter(NAME %in% c('Los Angeles',  'Long Beach', 'Anaheim', #'San Diego',  ## NOTE I'm excluding SD for this example
    'Riverside', 'Irvine', 'San Bernardino', 'Fontana', 'Moreno Valley',
    'Glendale', 'Ontario', 'Lancaster', 'Victorville', 'Newport Beach',
    'Buena Park', 'Redlands', 'Palm Springs', 'Claremont', 
    'Bloomington', 'Mead Valley', 'Santa Fe Springs')) |> 
  st_transform(crs = 4326)

placeRace <- SoCalEJ |> 
  st_intersection(project_places) # this clips the tracts to our place boundaries

leaflet() |> 
  addProviderTiles(provider = providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas) |> 
  addPolygons(data = placeRace,
              color = ~palW(white),
              fillOpacity = 0.8,
              stroke = FALSE,
              label = ~str_c(white, '%')
              )|> 
  addPolylines(data = project_places,
               color = 'black',
               weight = 2) |>  
  addLegend(data = placeRace,
            pal = palW,
            values = ~white,
            title = '% White') |> 
  setView(lng = -117.3, lat = 34.1, zoom = 8)


```

### `leafsync`

1) Make a map of each type we want to show.
2) Assign the map to a named variable.  In this case, we'll call the maps `white`, `hispanic`, and `aapi` and assign the leaflet maps to those variables using the `<-` operator.
3) Use the `sync()` function from leafsync to show them.

The code for steps 1 and 2 are just slight variations on the white map we showed above, repeated three times.  

@fig-leafsync shows the end result.  

```{r}
#| label: fig-leafsync
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: leaflet maps 

white <- 
  leaflet() |> 
  addProviderTiles(provider = providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas) |> 
  addPolygons(data = placeRace,
              color = ~palW(white),
              fillOpacity = 0.8,
              weight = 1) |> 
  addLegend(data = placeRace,
            pal = palW,
            values = ~white,
            title = '% White')

hispanic <- leaflet() |> 
  addProviderTiles(provider = providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas) |> 
  addPolygons(data = placeRace,
              color = ~palW(hisp),
              fillOpacity = 0.8,
              weight = 1) |> 
  addLegend(data = placeRace,
            pal = palW,
            values = ~hisp,
            title = '% Hispanic')

asian <- 
  leaflet() |> 
  addProviderTiles(provider = providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas) |>  
  addPolygons(data = placeRace,
              color = ~palW(asian),
              fillOpacity = 0.8,
              weight = 1) |> 
  addLegend(data = placeRace,
            pal = palW,
            values = ~asian,
            title = '% Asian')

black <- 
  leaflet() |> 
  addProviderTiles(provider = providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas) |>  
  addPolygons(data = placeRace,
              color = ~palW(black),
              fillOpacity = 0.8,
              weight = 1) |> 
  addLegend(data = placeRace,
            pal = palW,
            values = ~black,
            title = '% Black')

## This shows all four maps together
sync(white, hispanic, asian, black)
        
```

The cool thing about sync is it zooms in and out as a combination, so if they are all on the same scale, we can really see some differences.  

### Spatial Aggregates

Let's calculate the racial and ethnic percentages by municipality (excluding San Diego).  

One might assume that it is a straight average by jurisdiction.

```{r}
#| label: estimate municipal demographics
#| echo: true

placeRace |> 
  st_set_geometry(value = NULL) |>  #remove the geometry
  group_by(NAME) |> 
  summarize(white = round(mean(white),1),
            hispanic = round(mean(hisp),1),
            asian = round(mean(asian),1),
            black = round(mean(black),1)
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(hispanic)) |> 
  select(NAME, hispanic, white, asian, black)

```

This is an ok first cut, but is inaccurate because census tracts are not equal in population. 

The more correct method requires an extra couple of processing steps.

```{r}
#| label: more accurate municipal demographics
#| echo: true

placeRace |> 
  st_set_geometry(value = NULL) |>  #remove the geometry
  select(NAME, ACS2024Pop, white, black, asian, hisp) |> 
  mutate(white2 = white*ACS2024Pop/100,
         black2 = black*ACS2024Pop/100,
         asian2 = asian*ACS2024Pop/100,
         hisp2  = hisp*ACS2024Pop/100) |> 
  group_by(NAME) |> 
  summarize(white3 = sum(white2),
            black3 = sum(black2),
            hisp3 = sum(hisp2),
            asian3 = sum(asian2),
            totalPop = sum(ACS2024Pop)) |> 
  mutate(white = round(100*white3/totalPop,1),
            hispanic = round(100*hisp3/totalPop,1),
            asian = round(100*asian3/totalPop,1),
            black = round(100*black3/totalPop,1)
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(hispanic)) |> 
  select(NAME, hispanic, white, asian, black)

```
